July. Andrei has won a scholarship for a summer drawing course in Madrid. He’s staying with Carmen, Ana’s mother. On the first evening he goes out with Carlos and Hanako from the club.
Andrei, mate! How was your first day? Do you like Madrid?
Er… yes, I like it. I think. What exactly does “mola” mean?
Ha-ha. “Me mola” is “I like it”, but more informal. Carlos talks like a fifteen-year-old.
Hey, I’m thirty-two. But I’m young at heart. Right, how’s the course?
Amazing. The teacher is very good. But the first exercise was hard: drawing an old lady on the metro without her noticing.
Eaten bread? What’s bread got to do with it?
It means it’s very easy. Like in Romanian… how do you say it? “Floare la ureche”, isn’t it?
Floare la ureche! How do you know that?
Mihai taught me. Right, and how are things with Carmen? Is she treating you well?
Too well. She calls me “Andreíto”, gives me a little sandwich for the course and asks me every five minutes if I’m hungry.
Ha-ha. She’s the typical Spanish grandma. You’ll get used to it. Right, shall we meet up on Saturday? There’s a cool concert in the Retiro.
OK. But first I have to get my act together with the drawing of the lady on the metro. I have to hand it in tomorrow.
Look at that! You already talk like someone from Madrid. In a month, nobody will believe you’re Romanian.
“sin que se diera cuenta” = without her noticing (imperf. subj.)
“te acostumbrarás” = you’ll get used to it
“ponerme las pilas” = to get my act together
BA-leh: the most used word in Spain. It means “OK, fine, agreed”. Spaniards say it dozens of times a day.
The stress falls on the -I-: a-bweh-LEE-ta, mo-men-TEE-to, an-dreh-EE-to.
GWAI: a single syllable. Said with enthusiasm: «¡Qué guay!»
A diminutive shows that something is small OR that you’re fond of it. Spaniards use them a lot, especially with children, with family and to soften a request.
English has only a few diminutives (doggie, booklet, piglet). Spaniards use them everywhere, even with adverbs (ahorita, cerquita) and in polite requests (¿Me das un poquito de agua?).
Some diminutives have become new words: pasillo (corridor), bocadillo (sandwich), ventanilla (ticket window), mantequilla (butter). They’re not “small” any more!
“¡Qué cochazo!” = What a car! The augmentative often expresses admiration.
3. Young people’s colloquial Spanish in Spain
Colloquial language is for friends! Don’t say “¡Qué guay, tío!” to a director. And “tío” also means “uncle”: context decides.
to be up to your nostrils
costar un ojo de la cara
to cost an eye from your face

Some expressions are close to English ones: “costar un ojo de la cara” ~ “to cost an arm and a leg”, “echar una mano” ~ “to lend a hand”, “tomar el pelo” ~ “to pull someone’s leg”. Use the similarities!

Monday: Dad, I’m in Madrid now. Carmen’s place is a little house, but very pretty. She’s super kind. She made me a giant tortilla.

The exercise was simple, in theory: draw a stranger on the Madrid metro without them noticing. For Andrei, who had been drawing in secret all his life, it should have been a piece of cake.
But the Madrid metro was nothing like Bucharest’s. It was faster, noisier and more chaotic. People got on and off non-stop. Nobody stayed still for more than two stops.

On the first day, Andrei started four drawings and finished none. A man in a tie got off at Sol. A girl with headphones got off at Callao. Two German tourists noticed straight away and asked him to do their portrait. For free, of course.
The next day, Andrei got on the longest line, which crossed the whole city. He sat in a corner with his sketchbook and waited.

At the third stop an elderly lady got on. She was wearing a flowery dress, carrying a huge handbag and waving a black fan non-stop. She sat right opposite him. Her face was full of wrinkles and she had small, very lively eyes.
Andrei started drawing. First the outline of her face. Then her hands, which were big and strong, the hands of someone who had worked hard. Then the fan. Then the eyes.
The eyes took him longest. Every time he looked up, the lady was looking out of the window. Every time he looked at the page, he felt as if she were looking at him.
After ten stops, the drawing was almost finished. Only one detail was missing: the mouth. Andrei looked up one last time.
The lady was looking straight at him. And smiling.
“You’ve been drawing me for twenty minutes, lad,” she said, without stopping fanning herself. “Are you going to show me the result or do I have to imagine it?”
Andrei went redder than a tomato. He wanted the ground to swallow him up. But there was no escape: the train was between two stations.
“I’m sorry, madam. It’s an exercise for my course. You weren’t supposed to notice.”
“Son, I’ve been selling lottery tickets at the Puerta del Sol for fifty years. I notice everything. Come on, show me. I won’t be cross.”
Andrei handed her the sketchbook. The lady looked at it for a long time, in silence. The fan stopped for the first time.
“You’ve drawn my mother’s hands,” she said at last, her voice cracking a little. “She sold lottery tickets too. In the same spot. She had these hands.”
Then she looked at him curiously. “You’re not from here, are you? You’ve got a funny little accent.”
“Romanian! Well, my neighbour on the fifth floor is Romanian. She makes sarmale to die for. Do you know what sarmale are?”
Andrei burst out laughing. For the first time since arriving in Madrid, he felt at home.
Her name was Doña Paquita. She was seventy-eight and had indeed been selling lottery tickets for half a century at the Puerta del Sol, next to the statue of the bear and the strawberry tree.
Before getting off, she asked Andrei to sign the drawing and give it to her. Andrei hesitated: he needed it for his course. Doña Paquita thought for a moment.

“All right. Here’s what you do: take it to your course. And tomorrow, when you finish, come and see me at Sol. I’ll give you a lottery ticket for the drawing. You never know, lad. Maybe you’ll win and get rich.”
The next day, the course teacher looked at Andrei’s drawing for a long time. Then he hung it on the wall, in front of the whole class.
“This,” he said, “is what I want you to learn this summer. Not to draw faces. To draw stories.”
“But the lady noticed,” Andrei confessed, ashamed. “I didn’t do the exercise properly.”
The teacher smiled. “The best portrait is the one the person recognises. You got the exercise wrong, but you got what matters right.”
That afternoon, Andrei went to the Puerta del Sol. Doña Paquita was in her usual spot, with her fan and her box of tickets. When she saw him coming, she raised her hand.
Andrei gave her the drawing, signed. She gave him a lottery ticket with the number 15115.
“That’s the day your teacher’s little girl was born, isn’t it? You told me yesterday on the metro. Fifteen, one. For luck.”
Andrei didn’t win the lottery. But that summer, every afternoon after his course, he stopped by the Puerta del Sol to say hello to Doña Paquita. She told him stories about Madrid. He drew her.

By the end of the summer, he had a whole sketchbook of drawings of a lottery seller. And when Ana saw it in Bucharest in September, she said it was the best book she’d read in a long time. Even though it didn’t have a single word.

On the last day of the course, Andrei went to say goodbye to Doña Paquita. She was waiting for him with a plastic bag full of things: a black fan for his mother, a box of polvorones for his father and a sealed envelope.
“Don’t open the envelope until you get home,” she told him. “And don’t cry, lad, or your face will go like a tomato.”
Andrei didn’t cry. Well, just a little bit. On the plane, though, he couldn’t wait any longer and opened the envelope. Inside was a handwritten letter, in large writing full of spelling mistakes.

“Andreíto: I can’t draw and I can’t write properly either. I only went to school until I was ten, because I had to help my mother with the lottery. But I know how to look at people. I’ve been looking at them for fifty years.”

“And I’ll tell you something: you have the eyes of someone who’s going to go far. Don’t let anyone tell you drawing isn’t a profession. My mother sold little bits of paper with numbers on them and fed six children. You can live from your drawings.”
“P.S.: Tell your father I bought ticket number 15115 too. If it wins, we’ll split it fifty-fifty.”
At Bucharest airport his parents were waiting for him. Mr Dan was wearing his grey jacket, as usual. But this time he was holding a handmade sign, with clumsy letters: “WELCOME HOME, ARTIST”.

Andrei stood frozen in the middle of the arrivals hall, with Doña Paquita’s bag in one hand and his sketchbook in the other. Then he burst out laughing and crying at the same time, like that day at the bridge exhibition.
“Dad,” he said, in Spanish, without thinking, “¡qué guay!” (how cool!)
Mr Dan sighed, hugged him tight and answered, also in Spanish: “We’ll have a talk about your vocabulary, son. We will.”

Andrei makes a little dictionary of colloquial Spanish for his friends in Bucharest.
“¡Qué fuerte!”: you say it when something really surprises you. It has nothing to do with strength.
“Ir de cañas”: going out for small beers with friends. In Madrid it’s an almost religious activity.
“Estar en las nubes”: not paying attention. It happens to me in class when I’m thinking about drawing.
“Ser un rollo”: to be boring. Physics lessons are a drag. Sorry, Dad.
“Tener mala leche”: to have a nasty temper. Doña Paquita says the man at the kiosk next door has a very nasty temper.
